errors.description: The claimed basis is for the entire quotient, which is infinite-dimensional.
errors.evidence: The text claims {[1], [yu]} is a basis of Q[y,x0,x1,x2]/Jac(S). Setting all x_i to zero sends every generator G and yG_i of Jac(S) to zero, so this quotient surjects onto Q[y], and cannot have a two-element basis.

errors.location: The definition of μ preceding Example 2.8; Example 2.8
errors.description: The displayed formula forces μ=0, so the example's proposed real-cohomology description omits the conjugate Hodge component.
errors.evidence: The numerator is (∫γ1 ω)(∫γ2 ω) − (∫γ2 ω)(∫γ1 ω), which is zero by commutativity. Thus Example 2.8 reduces to C[1], while [1] lies in H^{1,0} and the elliptic curve also has a nonzero H^{0,1} component.

errors.description: As written, the theorem equates nonzero classes in distinct Hodge summands.
errors.evidence: Theorem 2.1 sends wt i to H^{n−1−i,i} and wt n−1−i to H^{i,n−1−i}. For even n these are distinct summands; since U_k is a basis element, the displayed equality of their images cannot hold. The displayed conclusion needs a conjugation on one side to express the stated goal.

errors.description: The stated freedom to choose any g is incompatible with identifying the unique conjugate class when the opposite Hodge summand has dimension greater than one.
errors.evidence: The theorem requires only that f_{j_i}g_{j_i} not lie in Jac(G), and the proof says it suffices to arrange the single scalar equality R(y^i f_{j_i}, y^{n−1−i}h_{j_i})=U_{k,γ}. One pairing value does not determine a vector in a higher-dimensional Hodge summand; changing g while preserving nonzero pairing generally changes the proposed class.

errors.description: The floor expression selects all middle-Hodge indices, making the claimed real-cohomology span too large when |I_m|>1.
errors.evidence: For the integer N=|I_m|, floor(N+1/2)=N. In the even-N branch of Corollary 2.7, each of these N middle indices contributes two real dimensions, giving 2s+2N, whereas μ=2s+N (with s=Σ_{i<m}|I_i|). For example, N=2 gives a span of dimension 2s+4 instead of 2s+2.
